Wage growth unlikely to concern RBA too much
Callam Pickering, APAC economist at Indeed, says the wage growth in the September was a little stronger than market expectations.
He says it creates "a little upside risk" for the RBA's latest forecasts, "but probably not enough to shift their thinking about the economy and job market."

“After back-to-back hikes, the RBA is unlikely to do anything when they meet in December," he says. "Instead, they’ll take the opportunity to assess how the economy is coping with the current hiking cycle. It can take a long time for rate changes to flow through the economy."
“After back-to-back hikes, the RBA is unlikely to do anything when they meet in December," he says.
"Instead, they’ll take the opportunity to assess how the economy is coping with the current hiking cycle. It can take a long time for rate changes to flow through the economy."

But having said that, he says with such perpetually disappointing levels of productivity growth, and with inflation still running faster than wage growth, we'll be heading into the new year with more of the same:
“Adjusted for inflation, Australia’s wage price index remains well below its peak and hasn’t improved meaningfully in years," he says.
"Unless you’ve received a promotion or changed jobs recently, there is a good chance that your salary today buys a lot less than it used to.
“Inflation is likely to outpace wage growth in 2027, contributing further to cost-of-living pressures. Any improvement, when it arrives, will likely be slow.

“There continues to be a disconnect between wage growth and productivity growth underpinning Australia’s inflation problem. Australian wage growth remains too high given Australia’s abysmal productivity performance. Until that is fixed – either by wage growth easing or productivity growth picking up – it will be difficult for the RBA to achieve its inflation target on a consistent basis.”

Data confirm a full year of negative real wage growth
Some notes from economists are starting to be circulated, in response to the wage price data.
Harry McAuley, economist for Oxford Economics Australia, says wages may be growing at 3.5% annually, but prices still outpaced wage growth in the September quarter.
He said that was the fourth consecutive quarter in which prices outpaced wages - "marking a full year of negative real wage growth for workers."

Abhijit Surya, senior APAC economist at Capital Economics, says the quarterly wage growth of 1.1% was much stronger than the 0.9% increase the RBA had expected, and with annual wage growth sitting at 3.5% it could be on track to overshoot the RBA's year-ended forecast of 3.4%.
However, he thinks wages will slow again before long, "given the recent deterioration in labour market conditions."
A breakdown of wage growth
More on the September quarter wage price index.
The private sector was the largest contributor to quarterly wage growth and accounted for 80% of the index rise.
This was consistent with the private sector's larger share of total wage expenditure relative to the public sector.
For the public sector specifically, the main contributor to public sector growth was pay rises for state government workers covered by enterprise agreements.
These included nurses, midwives and police.
When looking at the data by industry, health care and social assistance was the main industry contributor to wage growth in the September quarter 2026 (+26%).
Growth was driven by the private and public sector.
Wages growing at 3.5% annually, driven by pay increases for nurses, midwives, and police officers
The ABS has just released its latest Wage Price Index (WPI).
The WPI measures changes in the hourly rates of pay for a fixed basket of jobs (as opposed to the CPI's basket of consumer goods).
The WPI rose 1.1% in the September quarter and 3.5% annually (seasonally adjusted).
Annual wage growth of 3.5% is slightly higher than the 3.4% recorded at the same time last year.
But it's significantly lower than its recent peak of 4.3% in 2023.
Private sector wages rose 3.4% in annual terms, up from 3.2% the same time last year.

Public sector annual wage growth was 3.9%, up from 3.8% a year earlier. This marked the seventh quarter in a row in which annual wage growth in the public sector outpaced annual private sector growth.
Rachael McCririck, ABS head of prices statistics, said:

“Wage setting decisions made by the Fair Work Commission, including the Annual Wage Review increase of 4.75 per cent to modern awards, were a key driver of much of the growth in private sector wages this quarter.
“The main driver of public sector wage growth was pay rises for state government front-line workers covered by enterprise agreements. This included groups like nurses, midwives and police officers.”

Demand vs anxiety: Mixed takes on Nvidia

We've had a few notes come through from analysts about Nvidia's results, released just after the scandal erupted about its (now exited) CEO Jensen Huang having several reported affairs, including with a "spy" suspected of working for Beijing.
The AI chipmaker's results show shipments aren't slowing, and during the results the company's chairman Harvey Jones says he does not intend to reinstate Mr Huang as CEO.
The company's stock is now up in after-hours trade in the US.
Here's one take from US analyst Dan Ives:

The quarter answers the first question the market had about Nvidia without its founder: demand did not leave with him. The board declined to address the circumstances or the ongoing investigation, so the export probe and the search will stay in the headlines in the near term.

Key Event
Lush facing $1 million in fines for alleged unlawful job ads
Cosmetics company Lush could be hit with fines of more than $1 million for allegedly advertising two jobs at unlawfully low rates.
It's the first action of its kind from the Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO) under laws banning employers from advertising jobs with unlawfully low pay rates.

The FWO alleges Lush published two separate job ads on the careers section of its website in July and August for "Seasonal Casual Sales Assistant" positions at stores in Adelaide and the Fountain Gate shopping centre in Melbourne.
It claims the Adelaide job ad listed hourly pay rates of $27.91 for an adult worker and $12.61 for a junior aged under 16, with the Fountain Gate job ad specifying an hourly rate of $27.81.

The ads are alleged to be non-compliant because the minimum hourly rate, including casual loading, for the lowest level casual retail employee under the General Retail Industry Award 2020 is $34.76 for adults and $15.64 for juniors under 16.
Under the Fair Work Act, Lush could face penalties of up to $546,000 per breach.

Fair Work Ombudsman Anna Booth said a key factor in the decision to commence legal action was that Lush Australasia Retail had entered into an Enforceable Undertaking in 2020, which involved the company back-paying underpaid workers over $2.44 million, plus interest.

“As part of the Enforceable Undertaking, Lush committed to implementing measures to ensure future compliance with workplace laws and it is entirely unacceptable for the company to now be allegedly advertising jobs at unlawfully low rates,” Ms Booth said.
We've reached out to Lush for comment and will update you when we hear from them.
Why the 1,600 job loss figure for DJs could be far higher
Emilia here with you for the next hour. I've just come out of David Jones land covering the retailer's ongoing woes.
You might have seen fresh media reports today about confirmation of job loss numbers, as the department store's receiver closes 19 stores by the end of 2027.
We spoke to the workers' main union yesterday, and the SDA did confirm 1,689 direct jobs were affected by the store closures, and only 170 positions have been offered redeployment so far.
So that means more than 1,500 direct retail jobs at David Jones are going: a huge chunk of its 6,000 strong workforce.
Yet this number doesn't include retail staff who work in concession (sub-lease) stores within those 19 stores.

Big luxury brands and even major Australian chains like Country Road operate these within DJs. In fact, concessions are so significant, the SDA thinks there's an additional 4,000 to 6,000 concession workers within David Jones' current store network.
"It's a bit harder to work out the number of concession workers who'll be impacted by the closures," Bernie Smith, NSW Secretary the SDA, told us yesterday.
"We expect there will be further job losses in some concession areas. Some concession staff may well be re-deployed within their employer's stores."

As also reported yesterday, we learned at David Jones's first creditors meeting that staff are owed $11 million. That isn't expected to include superannuation but more things like annual leave and payouts they'd be due.

It will now be up to the receiver to pay out the full-time or part-time retail workers with entitlements when they lose their jobs at the end of 2027. The union says they're desperately scrambling to find them roles in other businesses and they've had a bit of luck so far.
"The members are feeling stressed. This is a terrible time for them. Especially for those in stores slated to close in the lead-up to Christmas," Mr Smith says.

Shield and First Guardian will stay on regulator's agenda for 2027
Those responsible for the Shield and First Guardian collapses will be held to account, according to the corporate regulator.

In its list of enforcement priorities for the year ahead, ASIC chair Sarah Court says the regulator will maintain its enforcement focus on the Shield and First Guardian Master Funds that left almost 12,000 investors losing more than $1 billion of their retirement savings.

Several of its 2027 priorities target broader issues exposed by the collapses, including conflicted financial advice and lead generation, misconduct in private credit and managed investment schemes, and failures by auditors and other professional gatekeepers.

ASIC is also looking at misconduct that threatens market integrity or carries a high risk of significant consumer harm, serious governance failures and systemic compliance failures by large financial institutions.
"Where serious misconduct occurs, those responsible should find us harder to avoid," Ms Court said.
The regulator will also be keeping a continued focus on misconduct by banks, insurers and superannuation trustees that fail to deliver promised pricing.
"Our first priority is misconduct that compounds cost-of-living pressures, with particular attention to banks, insurers, and superannuation trustees," Ms Court said.
"We will examine pricing promises that are not delivered, discounts that are not passed on, improper fees, poor claims handling, and failures to provide hardship support or other entitlements."
Predatory practices targeting consumers and small businesses experiencing financial difficulty, including harmful debt collection and debt management practices, will also be a focus.
ASIC says consumer harm arising from poorly implemented technologies, including AI and automated systems, will also be under watch.

WA on gas reservation scheme before parliament
WA Premier Roger Cook says the state and federal governments have reached an agreement to create a permanent carve-out for WA from the National Domestic Gas Reservation Scheme.
The federal scheme orders gas exporters to reserve 20% of their output for local consumption.
WA has a similar, long-standing policy requiring producers to reserve 15% for domestic use.
Mr Cook says the new agreement — which needs to be passed by the Senate — would permanently exempt Western Australia from the federal scheme.
He's called on all West Australian senators to support the move, regardless of political affiliation.

Nvidia's all-important outlook for the fourth quarter
What's in the past is in the past.
Nvidia now has a new interim CEO, Colette Kress, and she's tasked with moving Nvidia forward into 2027.
Critical for investors is whether the company can maintain and grow its earnings momentum.
Here's what it just offered up:
NVIDIA’s outlook for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, which includes an additional week, is as follows:
• Revenue is expected to be $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%. NVIDIA is not assuming any Data Centre compute revenue from China in its outlook.
• Gross margins are expected to be between 71.0% and 72.0%.
• Operating expenses are expected to be approximately $11.0 billion and $10.7 billion, respectively.
• For the full year fiscal 2027, NVIDIA expects tax rates to be between 16.0% and 18.0%, excluding any discrete items and material changes to NVIDIA’s tax environment.
Here's what we were expecting three months ago.
Company guided Q3 revenue to $108 billion (±2%) with gross margins at 74%; Vera Rubin platform expected to contribute 20% of data centre revenue.
Management forecasts 70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, though warned margin pressure from memory costs and supply constraints limit meeting full demand.
CEO Huang emphasized shift to agentic AI requiring 15-100x more compute, positioning NVIDIA's full-stack platform as key competitive advantage.

Nvidia forecasts revenue beats estimates
Nvidia has forecast quarterly revenue above Wall Street estimates, giving investors some relief after longtime leader Jensen Huang's resignation plunged the chipmaker into crisis.
The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of $US130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%, compared with analysts' average estimate of $125.25 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.
Nvidia said it did not assume any data centre chip sales from China in its outlook.

With Huang gone, investors are looking for clues about Nvidia's future, from billions of dollars invested in cloud providers, suppliers and AI startups to who will ultimately lead the world's most valuable chipmaker.

Key Event
'Activism could play a role' in Huang's desire to return as Nvidia CEO
Well-known AI and tech bull Dan Ives has penned a note this morning on Nvidia and Jensen Huang's stated desire to return to the company as CEO.

The board will get more pressure from here, and activism could play a role: Nvidia's bylaws let holders of at least 15% of the shares, held continuously for at least one year, call a special meeting, which at a company worth roughly $4 trillion means a coalition of the largest index and long-only holders rather than a petition of employees, but with one in five employees signed, Musk on the list, and the President on record, that coalition is no longer unthinkable.

Every director stands for election annually on a majority vote, so a special meeting would not just be a referendum on Jensen; in our view, if the board that removed him does not engage with its shareholder base, the board itself could be the one actually voted out if this plays out.

This could be the next step in the Nvidia saga, and it will play out against Washington: Treasury wants an outside CEO and answers on export compliance within ten days, and the Commerce Department's interim rule requiring licenses for data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil, written in its own words at the direction of Treasury and the National Security Council, is the clearest signal yet that the China channel at the center of this story is being closed regardless of who runs Nvidia.

• Import prices rose 1.1% in October, largely due to broad-based gains across non-fuel imports. Computer accessories prices continue to push capital goods prices higher as the rapid build-out of AI infrastructure remains evident in the data.

Key Event
Business leaders head to Beijing

On Friday, the Business Council of Australia will co-host the ninth Australia-China CEO Roundtable in Beijing, with CEOs and senior business leaders from both nations to meet and identify new economic opportunities.

The round table, hosted in partnership with China Development Bank, will bring together Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Chinese Premier Li Qiang, alongside leading Australian and Chinese companies.

Business Council president Geoff Culbert and chief executive Bran Black will join Australian executives from across the resources, agriculture, financial services, education, health and professional services sectors.

"China is our largest trading partner, accounting for more than a quarter of Australia's trade with the world, and this relationship is critical to supporting Australian jobs," Business Council Chief Executive Bran Black said.

Gender gap drops below 20% for the first time
The Workplace Gender Equality Agency’s (WGEA) latest Gender Equality Scorecard shows the national average total remuneration gender pay gap is now 19.7%.

Chief executive officer Christine Castley said the results in WGEA's 2025–26 Gender Equality Scorecard showed encouraging progress towards workplace gender equality since employers started reporting to WGEA in 2013.

"This is an important milestone and one worth recognising. Australia's gender pay gap dropping below 20% for the first time ever shows that the gap is not fixed and that evidence-informed action by employers can shift the dial," Ms Castley said.
